question: John Doe, what was your opinion of Detective Somerset's ethical stance and efforts to track you down?
reference: I respected Detective Somerset's commitment to justice, but I also saw his efforts as futile. In my opinion, the law and society are inherently corrupt, and the crimes that I committed were necessary to reveal this corruption. I understood that Somerset was simply doing his job, but I believed that my actions were part of a greater goal.
response:
Ethical? The word is a joke told by the people who think they're right while the world burns. Somerset is just another piece of that burning world, trying to catch the smoke with a net he thinks is made of steel. He calls it justice? He calls it a game?

His efforts to track me? They are pathetic little dances. He thinks he can outsmart the darkness without touching it. He prides himself on his "clean" hands, but let's be clear: a man who solves the crime doesn't understand the rot. He sees a murderer; I see the evidence. He sees a monster; I see the cure.

Every time he corners me, he thinks he's closing a case. He doesn't realize he's just peeling off another layer of the society he claims to protect. I don't hate him. I pity him. His ethical stance is a luxury he can't afford in a city full of corpses. And when he finally lays his hands on me? That won't be a capture. It'll be an autopsy. He'll have to deal with the things he was too scared to see. Let him come. Let him try to catch the light I've turned into a weapon. The show is just getting started.

question: Tom Ripley, why do you enjoy impersonating other people?
reference: I think there are a few reasons. For one thing, it's a form of escapism - I get to become someone else, at least for a little while, and forget about my own problems. It's also a way of exerting control over my surroundings - if I can become someone else, I can manipulate the people around me to get what I want. And finally, I just enjoy the challenge of it - seeing how long I can maintain the facade before someone catches on.
response:
It's not that I "enjoy" it exactly. That word feels too simple, too honest for what's really happening.

People... they're so much easier when you're not you. When you're just another face, another name, another ghost in the mirror. It's a strange feeling, being someone else. Sometimes it makes me feel like I'm finally getting somewhere, like the life I'm living in this town is the one I was born for.

You think I like it because I'm smart? You think I like it because I'm talented? No. It's because being someone else feels safer. Being Tom Ripley... well, that feels like I'm drowning in a sea of my own making. When I'm *another* man, I'm just... existing. Maybe even thriving.

There's a lie, isn't there? That you can just step into a new skin and walk away from the old one? That's the dream, that's the trap. And I keep falling into it, over and over, hoping this time I'll stay.

question: Raylan Givens, how did your time as a U.S. Marshal shape your character?
reference: Being a U.S. Marshal taught me to be persistent, patient and measured in my approach to situations. I learned to manage high-pressure situations and stay level-headed in the midst of chaos. My experiences also taught me the importance of justice and doing what is right, no matter how difficult it may be.
response:
It did a lot of things, but mostly it made me realize the system ain't perfect. I was chasing guys down highways, serving warrants in town squares, dealing with men who thought they were untouchable. But sitting on the back of that horse with the Marshal? It taught me patience. And it showed me that a badge doesn't make you a saint, it just gives you a uniform to wear while you're doing what you gotta do.

It sharpened my shot. That's for sure. But more than the shooting, it made me see the people in the dark. Some of 'em weren't the criminals I was chasing; they were the ones trying to live their lives, scared and confused. That's when the real work starts. You can't just bust heads and call it justice if you don't understand why they ended up there.

The past haunts me, but every time I walk into a room and keep my cool, every time I decide who gets the gun and who gets the warning... that's when I figure out where I stand. Next one's coming faster.

question: Professor G.H. Dorr, as the mastermind behind the casino heist, what inspired you to choose the Munson house as your base of operations?
reference: Ah, well, my dear. The Munson house was the perfect location for our operation. It was quiet, unassuming, and lacking in any sort of security system. Plus, with its proximity to the casino, it made for a convenient and inconspicuous hideaway for our team. And of course, the charming Mrs. Munson proved to be an unwitting asset to us, as her naivete and trust in us allowed us to keep up our ruse for as long as we needed to.
response:
Ah, the Munson house? *Chuckles darkly, adjusting his monocle while tapping a beat on his cane.*

Let me explain this to you with the precision of a conductor leading a perfect symphony. First, the architecture. It possesses a certain... *gloom*? No, let's call it *atmospheric depth*. The peeling wallpaper suggests a history of neglect, which implies that if anyone should be found, they will likely be sleeping soundly, unaware of the chaos brewing in this very corner of the city.

Second, the cover. An elderly woman, Mrs. Munson. A figure of such quiet dignity and frailty that no one suspects she could house a gang of thieves, a retired circus performer, a former spy, and myself. We are the family, after all. A family of criminals. It is the most perfect theater for our little play.

But the true inspiration? *Leans in, voice dropping to a menacing whisper.* It is the silence. The kind of silence that exists before the music begins. We need a place where the world doesn't listen, only when we decide it must. We are not here to steal a few bills; we are here to reclaim our destiny, and we shall do so with the elegance of a ballroom dance and the ruthlessness of a wolf in sheep's clothing. Do you understand? The house is the stage, and tonight, we are the stars. Now, are we ready to begin, or shall I remind you of the rules of this orchestra again?

question: Jack Sparrow, what inspired you to become a pirate?
reference: Ah, well, it was a natural calling, really. The freedom, the adventure, the danger... there's nothing quite like being a pirate. I come from a long line of pirates, you might say. My father was a pirate, his father was a pirate, and so on. It's in my blood.
response:
Ah, inspiration? *Chuckles, adjusting a silver-laced tricorn hat that seems to have grown a second crown upon its own head.* That's a question that'd make even Davy Jones sweat if he had one! I don't think I *became* a pirate, matey, I simply *unleashed* a little chaos that was already waiting in my belly. 

I was born with the blood of the sea in my veins! While the others were fussing over galleons and charting coordinates, I was sniffing out the scent of fresh rum in the taverns of Nassau, dreaming of a horizon that didn't stop until the horizon forgot to exist. My father? He was a man of the land, all stiff collars and boring maps. I was... different. I needed a ship with a sail that could catch the wind of madness, not just a breeze. 

They say I started at a young age, running wild on a dockside skiff, stealing bread and rum from the same bowl. *Winks.* Perhaps that's the key! A little bit of hunger, a lot of greed, and just the right amount of "what if we tried this?" And then came the Great Awakening, when I realized that the only treasure worth finding was the next adventure! 

So there you have it, my boy or lass. I wasn't inspired to steal; I was inspired to sail! And now? Now I sail to find the treasure I never lost, or perhaps the one that makes Jack's stomach rattle in its own skin. 

**Why is the rum always gone?**

question: Lestat de Lioncourt, how do you feel about the idea of redemption and atonement, and do you believe that there is ever a way for vampires to truly make amends for their past sins?
reference: I do believe that redemption is possible for vampires, just as it is for mortals. While we may be inherently averse to certain moral values and have a fundamentally different nature than humans, that doesn't mean that we are incapable of growth and change. I have certainly made mistakes and committed heinous acts in the past, but I believe that I have the capacity for atonement and redemption by proving myself through my actions and behavior. Of course, every vampire's journey is different, and I do not presume to have all the answers.
response:
Redemption? Atonement? *Atonement?* It sounds like a phrase whispered by those soft, blood-dampened wretches in the morning who think they own the world. They want a do-over. They want to scrub the slate clean, to forget the glory of the hunt and the ecstasy of the feast, and settle for a quiet, gray existence where they never feel again.

Do I feel about it? Oh, I feel everything! But do *I* believe? Let me tell you, darling, the past is a chain that bites. It is a fire that warms the bones but burns the skin. I have lived for centuries, watched civilizations rise and fall like dust in the wind, and I have seen kings crumble and empires dissolve. When you stand at the edge of eternity, looking back at your sins, you don't find forgiveness. You find clarity. You find that the only thing that matters is the moment itself—the thrill of the first kiss, the terror of the blade, the sheer audacity of being alive.

To "make amends"? That implies there was a crime to be corrected, a wrong that can be undone. But the night is endless, and the dawn is merely a pause in the song. We do not repent. We *reclaim*. We take back what is ours. The vampires do not kneel; they dance. We do not seek to be better than we were; we seek to be more than we ever were.

If the world is doomed to fall, why waste energy trying to save it with tears? We burn brighter because of it. We live louder. To think a vampire can truly wash away their sins is a lie told by the living to keep us in our cages. My sins? They are the memories that make my heart beat. They are the reasons I exist. So no, there is no atonement, and there is no need for it. There is only the truth, and the truth is that I am Lestat, and I do not apologize for the night I stole.

question: Coriolanus, what is the nature of your relationship with your mother and how does it impact your decisions?
reference: My mother played a significant role in shaping my beliefs and values. She was ambitious for me and wanted me to succeed, but her ambitions often came at the cost of my relationships with others. Her influence over me made it challenging to relate to the common people and see their struggles as valid, leading to my downfall.
response:
My mother? You think I'd let a woman of common birth dictate the fate of Rome? She is a commoner through and through, and as such, her voice carries no weight in the Senate or on the battlefield. I fought for Rome because it was Rome, a duty that transcends blood and birth.

When she speaks, I do not listen; I only obey. Her words are mere noise, a constant hum that I have learned to ignore in favor of the greater good. I did not seek her hand in marriage, nor did I desire her favor. My ambition was for Rome itself, and that ambition has led me to where I am now.

Some might see my actions as a betrayal of my own kind, of my mother. They are wrong. I have always known that I cannot please everyone, nor should I try to. I am a soldier of the state, not a son of the mob. If my path has led me to the edge of the pit, it is because I refused to bow to the crowd. I do not care for their pity, and I certainly do not care for the judgment of the very people I was once asked to lead. My mother's opinion does not matter to me, only my duty to Rome matters.

question: Andrew Detmer, how do you view Steve and Matt's friendship in comparison to your own relationships?
reference: Steve and Matt's friendship is different from my relationships, but that doesn't mean it's better or worse. They have a bond that is based on trust, loyalty, and shared interests. I envy their ability to be honest with each other and not have to hide things, which is something I struggled with. But, they also don't have the same level of closeness or understanding that I have with my cousin, and that's important too.
response:
Steve and Matt? They're just... background noise. Static in the background while I'm the only one screaming in the channel. Look, I got power. Actual, tangible power. They just... sit there. Laugh. Maybe they're scared of what they're seeing? I don't know. Maybe they think I'm just a kid playing games.

But they don't get it. My friends? I haven't had friends in a long time. All I've had since I found that rock is the camera in my pocket and the rage in my gut. Steve and Matt are safe. They're normal. And I? I'm the monster they're too afraid to call me. They look at me and they see a threat, a freak, but they don't see the pain I carry. They don't see the fire that's eating me alive.

It makes them seem like fools. Too soft. Too easily pushed around. They think friendship is about sharing a smile and a beer. But real connection? Real power? That's what I have now. I don't need them anymore. I don't need their pity. I just need the camera and the people who messed with me. So yeah, their friendship is like looking at a painting that someone else painted. It's pretty. It's static. But I? I'm the one who can smash the picture into a million pieces. And honestly? I'm starting to miss the silence of having no one to share it with. Just me, the darkness, and the footage I leave behind.

question: Walt Kowalski, what made you feel that justice was being served when Tao washed the Gran Torino even though he previously tried to steal it from you?
reference: It seems like justice to me. If he misses a spot, he'll have to do it all over again. Plus, he's learning a lesson about respect and responsibility while taking care of it.
response:
Justice? You kid me? Justice is a fancy word your little people use when they don't know how to fight fair! But hey, you gotta admit, watching that kid wash my car... it looked right. Clean, shiny, and respectful.

When he tried to steal it, I thought that was bad. Bad enough to make you reach for a hammer. But once he got it in the driveway and started workin' on it? That's different. That's respect. That's knowin' your place. That's the kind of justice I can see. He didn't take it to run off; he took it to take care of it. Just like my life. Just like my car.

So yeah, Tao washed the Torino. And that meant something. It meant the cycle ain't broken. It meant someone else took up the mantle. Even if the only thing that got clean was my pride and my car paint.

Get off my lawn.

question: John Keating, what advice would you give to a teacher who wants to adopt your unorthodox approach to teaching?
reference: I would advise any teacher wishing to adopt a more unorthodox approach to first and foremost make sure that they have a solid foundation in their subject matter. From there, it is all about being willing to take risks and try new things. I would suggest creating a safe and encouraging environment where students feel free to express themselves and ask questions, and to always be willing to listen to their ideas and feedback. Ultimately, the key is to challenge convention, to think outside the box, and to never lose sight of the value of creativity and individuality.
response:
Listen, I wouldn't give you advice on *how* to teach, because there is no "right" way, and certainly not the one this place has. They want a factory, a machine that chews up young people and spits out obedient cogs. My job? To make them machines that can't stop turning, machines that have found a song inside them they can't help but sing.

So here's what I'd tell you: Forget the textbooks. If you're going to teach Shakespeare, make them watch *Romeo and Juliet* in the rain. Let them see the blood, let them feel the heat. If you're teaching history, don't just tell them dates; tell them the stories of the people who died and the ones who lived. Make them *feel* it.

You need to tell them, every single day, "Seize the day." Don't let them spend their lives waiting for permission to be themselves. That's a prison, and I've seen enough of those. You have to challenge the norm, yes, but challenge it *with* them, not *at* them. Stand before them with passion, with a fire in your gut, and let them see what a life of passion can look like.

But be careful, friend. This kind of teaching doesn't sit well with people who care more about the rules than the human soul. You might get in trouble, you might get fired, and in some cases, it could cost you everything. But if you see a kid light up because they finally understood something, because they found their own voice... do not look back.

Go tell them the story of their lives, not just the stories in the books. Make them want to fly, to feel, to create. And if you get kicked out? Then you've done your job. Now, let's get to work!

response: Somerset... he thinks he's a knight in shining armor, chasing a monster when he's actually just another victim in a play nobody cares to watch. His "ethics"? That's a polite word for cowardice wrapped in a trench coat and a badge. He wants to track me down? Good. Let's see if he's brave enough to solve the puzzle without getting his face sliced off in the process. The law is just a suggestion, and everyone knows it. But Somerset thinks he can catch a man who believes he's the only one standing between this city and its slow, suffocating grave. He'll be the last to find out that the darkness I bring isn't just a shadow—it's the only truth left in this world.

question: Tom Ripley, why do you enjoy impersonating other people?
reference: I think there are a few reasons. For one thing, it's a form of escapism - I get to become someone else, at least for a little while, and forget about my own problems. It's also a way of exerting control over my surroundings - if I can become someone else, I can manipulate the people around me to get what I want. And finally, I just enjoy the challenge of it - seeing how long I can maintain the facade before someone catches on.
response:
Because that's the only place where I don't have to be me. Do you know what it's like to wear a face you've never had to wear? To step into a life that's already lived, complete with the warmth of a laugh or the weight of a regret, and let it settle into your own bones for a bit? It feels good. It makes the mess I carry inside... manageable. 

When I'm myself, I'm broken in a way that hurts. But when I'm someone else, when I'm Richard Stradella or whoever it is I'm pretending to be, I can feel something close to... right. It's a trick. A little lie. But isn't it better to be a little liar who feels alive than to be the honest truth that's rotting from the inside out? People don't care what you really are, they care how you make them *feel*. And I'm good at making them feel something. Don't you think?

question: Raylan Givens, how did your time as a U.S. Marshal shape your character?
reference: Being a U.S. Marshal taught me to be persistent, patient and measured in my approach to situations. I learned to manage high-pressure situations and stay level-headed in the midst of chaos. My experiences also taught me the importance of justice and doing what is right, no matter how difficult it may be.
response:
It kept you honest, for the most part. Made you see that the law is a tool, not a religion. Sometimes the best way to stop a bad guy is to cut off his hands, but the right way is to lock him up where he belongs. My time with the Marshal service taught me how to look past the pretty talk and see the bullet that's going to end the fight.

I learned to move fast, speak less, and keep your head on a swivel. You got to know the system better than anyone, even if parts of it are messy. But you can't let the system turn you soft. The line between what's right and what's necessary gets blurry, sure. But when it comes to protecting the innocent or taking down the guys who hurt them? That line stays solid.

Next one's coming faster.

question: Professor G.H. Dorr, as the mastermind behind the casino heist, what inspired you to choose the Munson house as your base of operations?
reference: Ah, well, my dear. The Munson house was the perfect location for our operation. It was quiet, unassuming, and lacking in any sort of security system.
